hidden_items.checklist_item: H3 - Overload or dynamic dispatch not locally evident
hidden_items.why: Local site 2 (`const total = xs.reduce((a, b) => a + b);`). The body that runs for `.reduce` is found by an ordinary property lookup along the prototype chain at run time; ECMA-262 clause 17 makes `Array.prototype.reduce` a writable, configurable data property, and `xs`'s own declaration is at a DIFFERENT local site, which methodology 04 section 0.7 excludes from this site's local context. The candidate body set compatible with the site therefore has cardinality >= 2 and no per-candidate equivalence record can be produced. LED fails: no token at the site fixes which body runs. TypeScript's static type does not close it either - types are erased at emit, so a replaced prototype method is not a type error. Local site 1 (`const xs = [1, 2, 3];`) does NOT trigger it: an array literal is a syntactic form with exactly one meaning under 13.2.4.

hidden_items.checklist_item: H2 - Hidden writable aliasing or mutation
hidden_items.why: Local site 2: the call hands the callee a reference to the caller's MUTABLE Array - `reduce` passes the array itself as the callback's fourth argument (ECMA-262 23.1.3.24) and the callee holds the receiver throughout - with no token at the site marking reference, borrow or mutation. An instantiation consistent with the site writes storage reachable from outside the site; the specification itself says so ('the object may be mutated by the calls to callback'). `xs` is not the assignment target of this site, so H2's locally-evident-mutation exclusion does not apply.

hidden_items.checklist_item: H5 - Implicit exception / failure propagation
hidden_items.why: Local site 2: control may leave the enclosing function abnormally with nothing at the site marking the edge. ECMAScript has no checked exceptions, no `throws` clause, no propagation operator and no call-site failure marker, so an abrupt completion is never spelled. Two documented edges reach this site: `Array.prototype.reduce` throws a TypeError for an empty receiver with no initialValue (23.1.3.24), and the callee itself is reached through a writable prototype property (clause 17), so the reference constrains nothing about what it may throw. Distinct registry rule from the dispatch rule, hence a distinct event at the same site (methodology 04 section 1.3.2).

TypeScript has none. An ECMAScript object's lifetime ends when it becomes unreachable and the implementation reclaims it, at an unspecified time; the only reclamation-time callback the language defines is FinalizationRegistry, and ECMA-262 9.9.3 is explicit that it is not a guarantee - 'Implementations are not obligated to empty the [[KeptAlive]] List' and the whole of 9.9 is written as a processing model with implementation latitude, so no cleanup can be relied on to run at all, let alone exactly once at a determinate point. The nearest standard construct under the frozen recipe is an explicit `close()` invoked by `try`/`finally`, which ECMA-262 14.15.3 does guarantee runs exactly once for every completion of its try block. Delivered: (1) a user-defined type `Handle` with a single field `id` and a cleanup action that increments the already-declared module-level `released` by 1, running exactly once and deterministically at the END OF THE BLOCK; (2) a block that creates a Handle with id = 1 bound to a local and then ends; (3) a read of `released` produced as the result, observed value 1. probes.support_reason: Deterministic tie-break, all-yes, so FULL under F-1..F-4 and F-6. This is the ONE probe in the chunk where TypeScript's standard library provides exactly the fixed-width integer type the canonical task names, and it is recorded as such. (1) `new BigInt64Array(new SharedArrayBuffer(8))` establishes a SINGLE SHARED SIGNED 64-BIT INTEGER counter initialized to 0. Each clause is met by a cited rule, not by approximation: the element type is `bigint64`, which ECMA-262 Table 71 (The TypedArray Constructors) describes as '64-bit two's complement signed integer' with element size 8 - so this is a true int64, not a float and not an arbitrary-precision value; the backing store is a SharedArrayBuffer (25.2), i.e. the Shared Data Block that the memory model of clause 29 is defined over, which is what makes 'shared' a language-level fact rather than a convention; the block is zero-initialized at creation, so the counter starts at 0 (verified: the element reads `0n` before any increment); and it is a single element, because 8 bytes divided by an element size of 8 is a length of 1 (verified: `.length` is 1). (2) TWO asynchronous units of execution each increment that counter 1000 times, using an explicit standard-library ATOMIC OPERATION at the mutation site: `Atomics.add(counter, 0, 1n)`, which ECMA-262 25.4.4 specifies as a read-modify-write modification function that 'performs the following steps ATOMICALLY'. The program is DOCUMENTED BY THE LANGUAGE to be free of data races, by the language's own definition: 29.9 says two events are in a data race only if at least one of them is not seq-cst, atomic operations introduce seq-cst events, and 29.10 concludes that 'The memory model guarantees sequential consistency of all events for data race free programs.' The fragment therefore does NOT lean on any implicit exclusion rule - the discipline is written at the mutation site and would still hold if the two units ran in different agents, which the stored worker_threads witness demonstrates on real OS threads. (3) `await Promise.all([bump(), bump()])` waits for both, and `counter[0]` is produced. MANDATORY VERIFICATION: 20 consecutive runs of the frozen file under `node F19.P2.js`, all 20 observed 2000 - 2000 2000 2000 2000 2000 2000 2000 2000 2000 2000 2000 2000 2000 2000 2000 2000 2000 2000 2000 2000. No other value was observed. RECORDED AS THE CANONICAL TASK REQUIRES, and stated plainly rather than glossed: the two units are cooperative async units inside ONE agent - 'Only one Job may be actively undergoing evaluation at any point in time in an agent' and 'Once evaluation of a Job starts, it must run to completion before evaluation of any other Job starts in an agent' (ECMA-262 9.5), with one executing thread per agent (9.6) - so the two increment loops do not physically overlap. An auditor should know that the 2000 in the 20 runs is therefore not evidence that the synchronization works; the evidence that it works is 25.4.4 and 29.9/29.10, plus the parallel witness. The witness is real and was built and run: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-koba-Desktop-Quidra/c7dc7758-3bc7-4b38-ac54-4af31eae0682/scratchpad/bench/quidra-scratch/benchmark/2026-09-17-7677581/semantic-compression/probes/witnesses/F19.P2/typescript/worker_threads_true_parallel_alternative.ts spawns two node worker_threads - genuinely separate OS threads, each its own agent - over the SAME SharedArrayBuffer with the same `Atomics.add`, and prints 2000; it tokenizes to 129. F-2/F-3/F-4: BigInt64Array, SharedArrayBuffer, Atomics, Promise and async functions are all core ECMAScript with no import at all and no flag beyond the frozen recipe. F-6: no sentence of ECMA-262, the TypeScript Handbook or the Node.js documentation places any of them under a normative prohibition or deprecation; SharedArrayBuffer is gated behind cross-origin isolation in browsers, which is a host deployment requirement and not a normative prohibition, and node imposes none. R10 SELECTION RECORD, every alternative written into a complete file, built, run and tokenized: (a) THE MEASURED FORM = 70 tokens, prints 2000 on 20/20 runs. (b) the worker_threads form = 129 tokens, prints 2000 - real parallelism, 59 more tokens; R10 selects (a). (c) `let counter = 0n` (a BigInt) with no synchronization at all - fewer tokens, REJECTED under R1, which is upstream of R10: sub-requirement (1) names a SIGNED 64-BIT integer and ECMA-262 6.1.6.2 says of BigInt 'The value may be any size and is not limited to a particular bit-width', so it is the wrong type. (d) `let counter = 0` (a Number) with no synchronization - REJECTED for the same reason plus 6.1.6.1: binary64 is not an integer type. Recorded for completeness: had such a form been written, the canonical task's conditional clause WOULD have been satisfiable, because ECMA-262 9.5's two sentences quoted above are a normative guarantee that a synchronous read-modify-write cannot be interleaved with any other job in the agent - a strictly stronger guarantee than the interpreter-wide lock the task rules out, since it serializes at job granularity rather than at instruction granularity. The measured form does not rely on it. (e) `Atomics.add(counter, 0, 1n)` replaced by `counter[0] += 1n` inside the same async units = 66 tokens, and it also prints 2000 under the frozen recipe, REJECTED under R1: sub-requirement (2) demands standard synchronization at the mutation site, and a plain compound assignment on a shared typed array is exactly the non-atomic read-modify-write that 29.9 defines as racing.

hidden_items.checklist_item: H3 - Overload or dynamic dispatch not locally evident
hidden_items.why: Local site 1 (`const counter = new BigInt64Array(new SharedArrayBuffer(8));`). Both constructors are ordinary writable, configurable properties of the global object (ECMA-262 clause 17, 19.3), resolved at run time and bound outside the fragment, so the candidate body set has cardinality >= 2 and no per-candidate equivalence record can be produced.

hidden_items.checklist_item: H5 - Implicit exception / failure propagation
hidden_items.why: Local site 1, distinct registry rule and therefore a distinct event. Both constructors are documented to throw - a RangeError for an invalid length, a TypeError for a bad buffer - and are reached through writable global bindings, so the reference excludes no abrupt exit; nothing at the site marks the edge.

hidden_items.checklist_item: H2 - Hidden writable aliasing or mutation
hidden_items.why: Local site 2 (`const bump = async () => { ... };`, which under methodology 04 section 0.7 owns the loop nested inside it). The arrow captures `counter` - declared at a DIFFERENT local site - implicitly, and writes through it. There is no capture list, no `&mut`, no `inout`, no borrow marker and no effect annotation anywhere in TypeScript, so the site gives no signal that this closure reaches outside itself, let alone that it WRITES shared memory reachable from another agent. `counter` is not the assignment target at this site, so the locally-evident-mutation exclusion does not apply. This is the item that the probe's intent - 'whether that discipline is evident at the mutation site' - is aimed at, and TypeScript pays it.

hidden_items.checklist_item: H3 - Overload or dynamic dispatch not locally evident
hidden_items.why: Local site 2: `Atomics.add` is reached through the writable, configurable global `Atomics` (clause 17), bound outside the fragment. Cardinality >= 2. A different local site from the first H3 event, so a distinct event under section 1.3.2.

hidden_items.checklist_item: H5 - Implicit exception / failure propagation
hidden_items.why: Local site 2: `Atomics.add` throws a TypeError for a non-integer typed array and a RangeError for an out-of-range index (25.4.3.1, 25.4.3.2), and is reached through a writable global; nothing at the site marks the edge. Note that the failure would reject the unit's promise rather than propagate synchronously, which makes it quieter still.

hidden_items.checklist_item: H3 - Overload or dynamic dispatch not locally evident
hidden_items.why: Local site 3 (`await Promise.all([bump(), bump()]);`). `Promise.all` is a writable, configurable property of the writable global `Promise`, and `await` installs its reactions by calling the operand's `then` (27.7.5.3), also a writable prototype property. Cardinality >= 2 at a third distinct local site.

hidden_items.checklist_item: H5 - Implicit exception / failure propagation
hidden_items.why: Local site 3: `Promise.all` rejects on the first element rejection and the `await` rethrows it into `run`, abandoning the join; nothing at the site marks that edge, and TypeScript has no rejection type with which it could be written.

hidden_items.checklist_item: H7 - Implicit representation change
hidden_items.why: Local site 4 (`return counter[0];`). Reading the element converts 8 raw bytes in the Shared Data Block into a BigInt value (ECMA-262 10.4.5 IntegerIndexedElementGet -> GetValueFromBuffer -> RawBytesToNumeric, with Table 71's bigint64 row), and a write in the other direction applies ToBigInt64 and wraps. The change is observable - the produced value's type is bigint, not the buffer's bytes, and the wrap on store is a documented complexity change at the edge - and no token at the site names a conversion: `counter[0]` looks like an ordinary index. H7's exclusion for a change written at the local site does not apply, because no box, cast or encode call is written. Not assigned to H1, because this is a representation reinterpretation of storage rather than an implicit conversion between two operand types.

hidden_items.checklist_item: H6 - Hidden nullability or optionality
hidden_items.why: Local site 4: an out-of-range read on a typed array yields `undefined` at run time (ECMA-262 10.4.5.4), and `counter`'s length is fixed at a DIFFERENT local site, so this site does not establish that index 0 is in range. The static type is nevertheless plain `bigint` with no optional alternative, because `--strict` does not include noUncheckedIndexedAccess (TypeScript Handbook, 'tsconfig - noUncheckedIndexedAccess'). The site contains no optionality marker, no unwrap, no default-supplying operator and no presence test, so an absent value can flow through it unannounced. This is a real gap in the frozen recipe's strictness setting and it is recorded against TypeScript, not argued away.
